background.definition: Pneumothorax (PTX) refers to a collection of gas in the pleural space that results in a collapse of the lung on the affected side. Pneumothoraces may be categorized as spontaneous, traumatic, or iatrogenic. Spontaneous PTX can be further subdivided into primary or secondary depending on whether underlying lung disease is absent or present, respectively. A tension PTX is a life-threatening condition caused by air within the pleural space that is under pressure, displacing mediastinal structures and compromising cardiopulmonary function.

list.listitem: Primary spontaneous PTX: 7.4 and 1.2 per 100,000 population per year for men and women, respectively.
Secondary spontaneous PTX (SSP): 6.3 and 2.0 per 100,000 population per year for men and women, respectively.
PTX occurs in 1% to 2% of all neonates.
Tension PTX occurs in 1% to 2% of the cases of idiopathic spontaneous PTX.
Iatrogenic PTX has been reported in a multitude of procedures, including accupuncture and breast augmentation.
The recurrence rate ranges from 16% to 52% in primary spontaneous PTX without definitive prevention, with most recurrences occurring within the first year.

Catamenial PTX is a rare phenomenon that generally occurs in women between the ages of 30 and 50 years. It accounts for 3% to 6% of PTX in menstruating women, ison the right side up to 95% of the time and frequently begins 1 to 3 days after menses onset.
COPD is most common cause of secondary spontaneous PTX.
Exercise is related to PTX in less than 10% of spontaneous PTX cases.
Idiopathic.
Trauma (penetrating and blunt).
Iatrogenic (eg, vascular access procedure).
Airway disease (eg, COPD, asthma, cystic fibrosis).
Infections.
Neoplasm.
Interstitial lung disease.
Connective tissue diseases.
Pulmonary infarction.
Endometriosis.

Tension PTX results from any lung parenchymal or bronchial injury that acts as a one-way valve and allows air into the pleural space but prevents its exit. Increase in pleural pressure causes mediastinal shift to uninvolved side, compromising venous return, and lowering cardiac output. Ventilation/perfusion mismatch results in hypoxemia.
Spontaneous PTX results from atraumatic rupture of alveolus, bronchiole, or bleb.
Respiratory bronchiolitis in smokers may be the pathologic driving process in primary spontaneous PTX.
In ectomorphs, rapid increase in vertical size of thorax may affect intrathoracic pressure at lung apex and drive subpleural cyst formation.
Emphysema-like changes found in more than 75% of primary spontaneous PTX patients undergoing VATS.
Ten percent of patients with spontaneous PTX have a family history 20.

Chest pain quality, ST elevation, positive cardiac enzymes

Elevation of hemidiaphragm, bowel pattern in chest
Pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema, history of instrumentation, vomiting, and Hamman's crunch
Stridor, choking/coughing, suggestive history of aspiration
Diffuse ST elevation, pericardial fluid visualized on ultrasound

Bilateral infiltrates on CXR, PaO2:FiO2 <200, PCWP <18
Normal CXR, possible psychiatric history, normal oxygen saturation
Reproducible chest wall pain with no other discernable causes

list.listitem: A small PTX is defined as one with less than 3 cm of collapse.
Classic presentation is dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.
Tachycardia is the most common physical finding, but it is very nonspecific.
The severity of symptoms is generally proportional to size of the PTX. Severe symptoms and evidence of respiratory distress suggest tension pneumothorax.
In SSP, dyspnea is often severe and out of proportion to the size of the PTX.
Tracheal deviation and hypotension are usually late findings in tension PTX.

Standard erect CXR in inspiration is the recommended initial study. Identification of the visceral pleural line displaced from the chest wall on an upright CXR is key to diagnosis. Distinguishing a PTX from a cyst or giant bulla, particularly in patients with SSP secondary to COPD, is also important.
Expiratory CXR adds little diagnostic sensitivity over a routine inspiratory film. In multisystem trauma, the CXR may not show an occult PTX in up to 55% of cases.
Obtain serial CXRs (every 4-6 hours) in penetrating chest wounds to rule out delayed PTX.

Ultrasound is more sensitive than CXR and is helpful when the diagnosis remains in question in a patient with a negative CXR result. However, patients with COPD may be at risk for false-positive ultrasound images, and accuracy declines more than 24 hours beyond insertion of a thoracostomy tube.
Ultrasound findings are based on analysis of artifacts including sliding lung sign, A and B lines and the lung point.

CT may reveal a potential underlying pathophysiologic cause of SSP and is considered the reference standard for diagnosis of PTX when the diagnosis is in question. CT often identifies occult pneumothoraces (OPTXs); OPTXs are often located at easily accessible windows.
ECG is often necessary to rule out cardiac etiology.
Hypoxemia is common due to alterations in ventilation-perfusion relationships.
PTX must be considered in a patient with dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, especially of sudden onset. If suspected, order a CXR.
Emergent needle thoracostomy should be performed if patient is hemodynamically unstable and findings are consistent with tension PTX.

Therapy should be guided by patient's clinical status, not solely by radiographic size of PTX. For patients with small primary spontaneous pneumothorax and no significant shortness of breath, observation is the treatment of choice.
See for management of primary and SSP.
The goals of therapy are to eliminate intrapleural air collection and attempt recurrence prevention, if indicated. B
Suspected tension PTX requires either immediate needle thoracostomy or tube thoracostomy. C
Determine management by PTX size, severity of symptoms, presence of air leak, and type of PTX. B
Observation is the recommended treatment for patients with primary spontaneous pneumothorax and no significant shortness of breath. B
Local administration of lidocaine is recommended prior to performing a tube thoracostomy.
Analgesics and benzodiazepines are useful for premedication prior to placement of a thoracostomy tube.

Minocycline pleurodesis following aspiration and drainage in patients with primary spontaneous PTX reduces recurrences within 1 year compared to aspiration and drainage alone, but this procedure also results in more pain.
See for tube thoracostomy indications and for an approach to the management of primary spontaneous PTX and SSP.

Simple aspiration using a 14- to 16-gauge catheter under local anesthesia is associated with a reduction in the percent of patients hospitalized when compared with intercostal tube drainage. Air is manually withdrawn until no more can be aspirated; suspect persistent air leak if you feel no resistance after 4 liters has been aspirated and lung has not fully expanded. Simple aspiration is less likely to succeed in patients with SSP than in those with primary spontaneous PTX.

British Thoracic Society guidelines (2010) recommend needle aspiration with a 14- to 16-guage as initial therapy, as it is just as effective as large bore chest drains (>20 French) and reduce length of stay and the need for hospitalization. If needle aspiration fails, a small bore (<14 F) chest drain is recommended. Routine use of suction is not recommended. If used, high-volume/low-pressure suction systems are recommended.
One study found no difference in post-chest tube removal PTX rates when comparing removal at end expiration or end inspiration.

Heimlich valves may facilitate an outpatient approach to care. The serial-steps approach involves the placement of a Heimlich valve for 24 to 48 hours, followed by wall suction. Heimlich valve placement may allow patients to return home and undergo follow up CXR and clinical assessment in 24 to 48 hours. Heimlich valve alone was found to have 85.5% initial success rate.In an open-label U.K. RCT of 776 adults with PSP comparing a Heimlich device to standard care, the intervention group had a significantly shorter duration of hospitalization and 30-day readmissions, but a higher rate of serious adverse events.

In a multicenter RCT of 316 patients presenting with a first PSP, conservative observation was noninferior to immediate chest tube insertion in achieving full lung reexpansion at 8 weeks, and led to fewer complications and shorter hospital stays.
SSP is PTX in patients with chronic lung disease. These patients should be admitted and treated with small bore (<14 F) chest tube.
They should be referred to a pulmonologist (chest physician) and most should be hospitalized for at least 24 hours.
Chemical pleurodesis or surgery should be considered for patients with recurrent PTX.

Traumatic PTX: The majority of patients with a traumatic PTX should be treated with tube thoracostomy. SSP patients should be treated with chest tube drainage. Unstable patients and those at risk for large pleural air leaks require 24F to 28F chest tubes.
Iatrogenic PTX: This may be managed by observation or small bore chest tube placement, depending on PTX size and clinical status.
Oxygen supplementation recommended for initial treatment.

Observation for 3 to 6 hours with supplemental oxygen may be used in clinically stable primary spontaneous PTX patients (first occurrence) with a small PTX; repeat CXR must exclude progression prior to discharge.
BTS guidelines recommend hospitalization and referral to a chest physician for all patients with secondary spontaneous pneumothorax.
Clinically stable patients with small primary spontaneous PTX may be admitted if they live distant from emergency services or follow-up care is considered unreliable.
Most stable patients with a large primary spontaneous PTX and all unstable patients should be hospitalized.
Suction is required when treatment with Heimlich valve fails. Aspiration catheter should be attached to 20 cm H2O pressure.

Reexpansion pulmonary edema (REPO), an uncommon complication after chest tube drainage of PTX, may be prevented by gradual drainage and the avoidance of negative suction, however many studies suggest that REPO is related solely to the size and duration of the PTX rather than prompt suction.
Treatment of REPO includes aggressive fluid resuscitation and supportive treatment.
Surgical intervention is indicated for air leaks that continue longer than 5 days; prolonged delays may decrease the effectiveness of thoracoscopy.
Videoscope-assisted thoracoscopic surgery is recommended for recurrence prevention and to correct a persistent air leak.
Recurrence prevention procedure is recommended at second PTX occurrence in primary spontaneous PTX and after first secondary spontaneous PTX occurrence.
Chemical pleurodesis via chest tube is an acceptable approach, though its success rates are lower than with surgical interventions.
Recurrence is usually not a factor in iatrogenic PTX.
Discharge instructions should include prompt return for new onset chest pain or dyspnea. C
Follow up in 24 to 48 hours for stable patients with small non-expanding primary spontaneous PTX or with secured catheter and Heimlich valve after successful aspiration. B
The rate of pleural air absorption without oxygen supplementation is approximately 1.25% per day of the involved hemothorax.
Recurrence is usually not a factor in iatrogenic PTX.
In two trials, videoscopic-assisted thoracoscopic surgery was associated with fewer recurrences than pleural drainage.
Perform a CXR at follow-up to assure reexpansion.
Follow up in 24 to 48 hours for stable patients with small nonexpanding primary spontaneous PTX or with secured catheter and Heimlich valve after successful aspiration. B
Avoid smoking and illicit drug use.
Do not fly until the episode of PTX is fully resolved. Diving is not recommended unless definitive therapy has been provided (bilateral surgical pleurectomy).
Preventative intervention is recommended after first primary spontaneous PTX if the patient has a job in which recurrence would be dangerous to him- or herself or others (eg, pilot, deep sea diver).
Discharge instruction should include prompt return for new onset chest pain or dyspnea.
